concept.body: Parallel lines have equal slopes — proved by TRANSLATING a slope triangle from one line to the other (translations preserve run and rise). Converse: through one point only one line has a given slope, so distinct same-slope lines can never meet. Shared endpoint + equal slopes = collinear points.

widget.prompt: Segment 1 runs (0,0) to (8,4); segment 2 runs (1,7) to (7,10). Compute segment 2's slope (decimal).

commonErrors.feedback: 2 = 6/3 inverts — rise over run: 3/6 = 0.5, matching segment 1.
3 is the rise alone — divide by the run 6: 0.5.

steps.body: Algebra 1 handed you the rule: **parallel lines have equal slopes**. Here's the missing WHY. Take any slope triangle on line ℓ and **translate** it (a rigid motion from Grade 8) until its corner lands on line ₘ. Translations preserve direction, so the image triangle's hypotenuse still points along ℓ's direction — if ₘ is parallel, it runs along ₘ exactly: same run, same rise, same slope.

widget.prompt: Segment AB runs from (0, 0) to (4, 3). Segment CD runs from (1, 5) to (9, 11). Compute CD's slope (as a decimal).

commonErrors.feedback: 1.33 ≈ 8/6 is run over rise — slope stacks RISE over run: 6/8 = 0.75, equal to AB's.
6 is the rise alone — divide by the run 8: 0.75.

steps.body: The converse needs one more idea: through a given point there's only ONE line with a given slope (pick the point, the slope forces every other point). So if two DISTINCT lines share a slope, neither can cross the other — a crossing point would put two same-slope lines through one point, collapsing them into one line. Equal slopes ⇔ parallel (or identical).

explanationVariants: From (2, 1) with slope 3/4: Δx = 8 forces Δy = 6, so y = 1 + 6 = 7.

widget.prompt: A line through (2, 1) is parallel to a slope-3/4 line. Find its y-value at x = 10.

commonErrors.feedback: 6 = (3/4)(8) is the RISE alone — add the starting height: 1 + 6 = 7.
11.67 rides the RECIPROCAL slope 4/3 — parallel copies the slope exactly: 1 + (3/4)(8) = 7.
8 reuses Δx as the rise — the slope scales it: rise = (3/4)(8) = 6, so y = 7.

explanationVariants: Translations preserve direction and distance — so the slope triangle arrives intact on the second line.
Rigid motion + preserved direction = equal rise/run on both lines.

widget.prompt: Which fact makes the translation proof work?

options.label: Translations preserve segment directions and lengths — the slope triangle lands unchanged on the parallel line
options.feedback: A translated triangle keeps its run and rise exactly, and parallel lines share direction — so the same triangle measures both slopes.

options.label: Translations rotate figures into alignment
options.feedback: Translations never rotate — preserving direction is precisely why the argument works.

options.label: Parallel lines are always horizontal
options.feedback: Any direction works — the triangle rides the translation at every tilt.

options.label: Slope triangles only exist on parallel lines
options.feedback: Every non-vertical line carries slope triangles — the translation shows parallel ones carry CONGRUENT triangles.

widget.prompt: Segments AB and BC share endpoint B and have equal slopes. What follows?

choices.label: A, B, C are collinear — same slope THROUGH a shared point means one line
choices.feedback: The uniqueness fact: one point + one slope = one line. Sharing B upgrades parallel to collinear — a workhorse test in coordinate proofs.

choices.label: They're parallel but separate
choices.feedback: Separate parallels can't TOUCH — sharing B forces them onto the same line: collinear.

choices.label: They must be perpendicular
choices.feedback: Perpendicular needs slopes multiplying to −1 — EQUAL slopes through a shared point collapse to one line.

choices.label: Nothing can be concluded
choices.feedback: Plenty follows: equal slope + shared point is the standard collinearity test.

widget.successFeedback: The uniqueness fact: one point + one slope = one line. Sharing B upgrades parallel to collinear — a workhorse test in coordinate proofs.
widget.explorationFeedback: Open at least two coordinate-proof states before checking.
widget.fallbackFeedback: Inspect the coordinate invariants, then choose the supported conclusion.

widget.prompt: Quadrilateral has vertices W(0,0), X(6,2), Y(5,6), Z(2,5). Slope WX = 1/3. Compute slope ZY (as a decimal) — the pair that decides trapezoid-hood.

commonErrors.feedback: 3 = 3/1 inverts — rise over run is (6 − 5)/(5 − 2) = 1/3 ≈ 0.33: parallel to WX, one parallel pair.
−0.33 flips a sign — both differences are positive: (6−5)/(5−2) = 1/3 ≈ 0.33.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Slope ZY = 1/3 = slope WX: one parallel pair — the exclusive-trapezoid verdict awaits the OTHER pair (it differs), a full proof in the next chapter.

hints: A parallelogram needs BOTH opposite pairs parallel — equal slopes twice.
From D, side DC must copy AB's displacement (parallel AND equal length): C = D + (B − A).
Compute B − A = (5, 2) and add to D.
explanationVariants: C = (1 + 5, 6 + 2) = (6, 8). Check both pairs: DC's displacement (5, 2) matches AB's, and BC's displacement (−1, 6) matches AD's — both slope pairs equal, a genuine parallelogram. Enter 6.
C = D + (B − A) = (6, 8); both displacement pairs match, so both slope pairs match.

widget.prompt: Parallelogram ABCD (vertices in order) has A(2, 0), B(7, 2), D(1, 6). Find C. Enter C's x-coordinate.

commonErrors.feedback: 8 = 7 + 1 adds B and D x-coordinates — C copies AB's displacement onto D: 1 + (7 − 2) = 6.
4 = (7 + 1)/2 averages B and D — that's the DIAGONAL midpoint's x, and C doubles past it: 2(4) − 2 = 6.
−4 subtracts the displacement (1 − 5) — C rides it FORWARD from D: 1 + 5 = 6.

widget.fallbackFeedback: C = D + (B − A) = (1 + 5, 6 + 2) = (6, 8) — equal displacements give equal slopes on both pairs.

steps.body: Equal slopes, at last with a warrant.
takeaways: Translation carries a slope triangle intact between parallel lines: parallel ⇒ equal slopes.
Uniqueness (one point, one slope, one line) proves the converse — and upgrades shared-point equal slopes to collinearity.
Parallelogram completion: copy the displacement, and both slope pairs follow.
steps.teaser: Next: the perpendicular rule — where a quarter-turn does the proving.
